subject: astronomy
topicDisplay: Early Models of the Solar System
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In the geocentric model of the Solar System, what lies at the centre?
questions.explain: The geocentric ('Earth-centred') model places a stationary Earth at the centre with all other bodies orbiting it.

questions.q: In the heliocentric model, which body is placed at or near the centre?
questions.explain: 'Helios' means Sun, so the heliocentric model has the Sun at the centre with the planets, including Earth, orbiting it.

questions.q: In Ptolemy's geocentric model, what name was given to the small circle on which a planet moved?
questions.explain: Each planet moved on a small circle called an epicycle, whose centre moved around a larger circle called the deferent.

questions.q: In Ptolemy's model, what was the name of the large circle around the Earth whose path the epicycle's centre followed?
questions.explain: The deferent was the large circle centred near the Earth, along which the centre of each planet's epicycle travelled.

questions.q: Which astronomer published a detailed geocentric model in his work known as the Almagest?
questions.explain: Ptolemy, working in the 2nd century AD, set out his epicycle-based geocentric system in the Almagest.

questions.q: In which year did Copernicus publish his major work setting out the heliocentric model, 'De revolutionibus orbium coelestium'?
questions.explain: Copernicus's heliocentric work was published in 1543, the year of his death.

questions.q: Which astronomer proposed that the planets move in elliptical orbits rather than perfect circles?
questions.explain: Kepler showed that planetary orbits are ellipses, replacing the circular orbits used by both Ptolemy and Copernicus.

questions.q: According to Kepler, an elliptical planetary orbit has the Sun located at which point?
options: The exact centre of the ellipse
The nearest end of the ellipse
questions.explain: Kepler's first law states that each planet moves in an ellipse with the Sun at one of the two foci.

questions.q: How many moons of Jupiter did Galileo discover with his telescope (the Galilean moons)?
questions.explain: Galileo observed four moons of Jupiter (Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto), now called the Galilean moons.

questions.q: Which astronomer used one of the first astronomical telescopes to observe the phases of Venus and the moons of Jupiter?
questions.explain: Galileo made pioneering telescopic observations from around 1609-1610 that supported the heliocentric model.

questions.q: Why did Ptolemy introduce epicycles into his geocentric model?
options: To account for the apparent retrograde (backward) motion of the planets
To measure the distance to the Sun
To explain the phases of the Moon
questions.explain: Epicycles allowed the geocentric model to reproduce the occasional backward looping of planets against the stars.

questions.q: How does the heliocentric model explain the apparent retrograde motion of an outer planet such as Mars?
options: Mars physically stops and reverses in its orbit
The faster-moving Earth overtakes Mars, making it appear to move backwards
Mars moves on a small epicycle around the Earth
Mars is briefly pulled backwards by the Sun
questions.explain: As Earth on its inner, faster orbit passes an outer planet, the planet appears to loop backwards against the background stars.

questions.q: Galileo observed that Venus shows a full cycle of phases, including a nearly 'full' gibbous phase. Why does this support the heliocentric model?
options: It proves Venus produces its own light
It shows Venus must orbit the Sun, not the Earth
It shows Venus is closer to Earth than the Sun
It proves the Earth is stationary
questions.explain: A full set of phases can only occur if Venus orbits the Sun; the Ptolemaic model predicted only crescent phases.

questions.q: Why was Galileo's discovery of moons orbiting Jupiter important evidence against the geocentric model?
options: It proved Jupiter was larger than the Sun
It showed that not everything in the sky orbits the Earth
It showed that Jupiter had no atmosphere
It proved the orbits were elliptical
questions.explain: Bodies clearly orbiting Jupiter contradicted the geocentric claim that all objects circle the Earth.

questions.q: What is the main difference between the models of Ptolemy and Copernicus?
options: Copernicus placed the Sun at the centre while Ptolemy placed the Earth at the centre
Copernicus used ellipses while Ptolemy used circles
Ptolemy included the outer planets but Copernicus did not
Copernicus removed the Moon from his model
questions.explain: Ptolemy's model was geocentric whereas Copernicus's model was heliocentric, though both still used circular motions.

questions.q: One reason many astronomers came to prefer the heliocentric model over Ptolemy's system was that it was:
options: Able to predict eclipses for the first time
A simpler explanation of retrograde motion without large numbers of epicycles
The only model that included the Moon
Based on direct measurement of the Earth's motion
questions.explain: The heliocentric model explained retrograde motion naturally, avoiding the many epicycles the geocentric model required.

questions.q: Copernicus's heliocentric model still had one important feature in common with Ptolemy's model. What was it?
options: It placed the Earth at the centre
It abandoned the idea of orbits entirely
questions.explain: Both Ptolemy and Copernicus assumed circular motion; it was Kepler who later introduced elliptical orbits.

questions.q: An observer using a telescope sees that Venus appears almost fully illuminated (a gibbous phase) at one time of year. Which conclusion does this support?
options: Venus lies between the Earth and the Sun at all times
Venus orbits the Sun, consistent with the heliocentric model
Venus orbits the Earth, consistent with the geocentric model
questions.explain: A gibbous Venus can only be seen if Venus passes to the far side of the Sun, which requires it to orbit the Sun.

questions.q: A student records the position of Mars over several months and finds it appears to move westward against the stars before resuming its normal eastward path. Using the heliocentric model, this loop is best explained by:
options: Mars slowing down and reversing its orbit
The Earth overtaking Mars on its inner orbit
Mars moving onto an epicycle around the Sun
A change in the Sun's position
questions.explain: The apparent westward loop is a line-of-sight effect caused by the faster Earth passing the slower outer planet.

questions.q: Place these astronomers in the correct chronological order of their main contributions, earliest first.
questions.explain: Ptolemy (2nd century AD) came first, then Copernicus (1543), followed by Galileo and Kepler in the early 17th century.
